children: Centrus Energy
surges 7% in Monday's trading as
The Wall Street Journal
's Heard On The Street column praised the company's "unique position" whose shares deserve an energy security premium.
Centrus

shares peaked late last year before losing steam this year alongside other nuclear stocks, but the company looks less speculative than other nuclear plays, according to Heard On The Street's Jinjoo Lee.
The stock still is not cheap, trading at 52x forward earnings, but Centrus'
market cap is less than half that of X-Energy
and Oklo
, both of which are small modular reactor companies that are nowhere near generating a profit, Lee noted.
Industry watchers say demand will not pose a problem for Centrus
— even though incumbents Urenco and Orano are expanding or adding enrichment capacity in the U.S. — as utilities want diversification, UxC President Jonathan Hinze said.

"Russian [supply] is going away, China is not supplying the West. Utilities in the U.S., Europe, Japan, and Korea want more options," according to Hinze, noting that South Korean utility Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power, for example, has signed a long-term supply agreement with Centrus
Centrus

expects most of its future enrichment revenues will come from low-enriched uranium, the type that conventional nuclear reactors use, but it is well positioned to benefit if SMR technology takes off, since it is the only company with a Nuclear Regulatory Commission license to produce the highly enriched uranium required by some of the new technologies.
The company's other potential market is the U.S. government, Lee said, noting that Centrus
is the only enrichment company that relies solely on domestically made components, making it the only player that can meet U.S. national security needs such as naval reactors.
While Centrus
has been lumped together with some more-speculative nuclear stocks, its technology is proven, and future revenues do not depend on new technologies taking off, Lee wrote.

title: Centrus Energy surges as WSJ's Heard On The Street touts as 'safer way to bet on nuclear'
